title: Score Mismatch and Set-Constrained Sampling in Zero-Shot Conditional Discrete Diffusion

paper.title: Score Mismatch and Set-Constrained Sampling in Zero-Shot Conditional Discrete Diffusion
paper.abstract: Abstract Discrete diffusion models have become a powerful framework for modeling complex discrete distributions across a range of applications. While theoretical convergence guarantees depend on consistency between the target and training distributions, such a case rarely holds in practice, making score mismatch a central challenge in discrete diffusion sampling. This is particularly relevant to zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is directly reused at inference time to sample from a conditional target distribution. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis for score-mismatched discrete diffusion models and derive a general KL divergence upper bound that clearly identifies the additional bias caused by such a mismatch. Our analysis covers partial-observation constraints, including text infilling, sentence completion, and more general coordinatewise set constraints. Specifically, we analyze the classical Conditional SEDD sampler and show that it can incur a bias term that scales with the dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility. Based on this analysis, we propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints. We show that the assignment probabilities can be expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Finally, numerical and real-data experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: In recent years, diffusion model has become one of the core paradigms in generative modeling and has achieved impressive success in image, audio, and text generation. Compared with the classical autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion models model the complex data distribution through gradual denoising, demonstrating the notable advantages in generation quality, stability, and flexibility [ 1 , 2 ] . For discrete data such as text sequences, discrete diffusion models extend this denoising principle to the discrete case by defining the noising and denoising processes directly on the discrete state space [ 3 , 4 ] . In an idealized setting, diffusion models are trained and evaluated on the same underlying distribution. However, in practice, this assumption often fails, as discrepancies between the training and target distributions can arise due to factors such as privacy constraints, computational limitations, and mismatches between the training setup and the intended sampling task [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . A representative example is conditional generation, where part of the data is observed and the goal is to infer the unobserved part. Many tasks involving discrete data fall into this category, including sequence completion and text infilling [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Such tasks include generating the subsequent content based on the given prefix and filling the missing content while preserving the context. We refer to conditioning on fixed values as sampling “under fixed observations.” More generally, each constrained coordinate may admit several candidate values, which leads to sampling under the coordinate wise set constraints. We call a feasible combination of values an “assignment”. For example, in text rewriting and lexical simplification, each position of the word can be associated with a set of candidate replacements [ 12 , 13 ] . Fixed observations are recovered when each set contains a single value. Compared to AR models, diffusion models are more naturally suited to these tasks, as they do not rely on a fixed generation order and can flexibly handle partially observed inputs. Within conditional sampling, one solution is to train a dedicated conditional diffusion model or adapt a pretrained model for each task, such as predictor-free guidance [ 14 ] and inference-time alignment methods [ 15 ] . However, such approaches may be costly because they require additional training of a new conditional model beyond unconditional pretraining. In comparison, zero-shot conditional generation does not require such an additional conditional model, since it directly uses the given condition at inference time to build a conditional sampler [ 9 , 10 ] . The core challenge for zero-shot conditional samplers is the inherent mismatch between the pretrained unconditional model and the conditional model needed in the inference process. In diffusion sampling, this discrepancy manifests in the score function, a phenomenon known as score mismatch [ 7 ] . Among all zero-shot conditional samplers, the Conditional SEDD method [ 9 ] is particularly relevant to this paper. At each diffusion sampling step, Conditional SEDD enforces the fixed observations by setting the corresponding components of the current sample to their observed values, an operation we refer to as “hard clamping.” Although this method is straightforward to implement in practice, we will show that it is not generally equivalent to the true conditional reverse process, thereby introducing bias. Moreover, this approach still lacks any theoretical justifications. This naturally raises the first question studied in this paper: Question 1: Can we characterize the bias induced by score-mismatched discrete diffusion models? Moving from fixed observations to set constraints introduces another challenge, that is, how to allocate sampling probabilities to each feasible assignment. Once an assignment is selected, the fixed-observation sampler can be reused to generate the remaining contents. After understanding the construction of the assignment distribution, in order to make the fixed-observation sampler better aligned with the target distribution given set constraints while preserving the main advantage of the zero-shot approach, the second question arises: Question 2: Can we design a novel method that extends the fixed-observation sampler to the set constraints setting, while explicitly controlling the additional approximation error? In this paper, we answer both questions affirmatively.

sections.heading: I-A Our Contributions
sections.text: Overall, our analysis focuses on how mismatched scores interfere with the reverse rate matrix, thereby introducing bias into the sampling process for both general and zero-shot conditional samplers. This analysis provides the convergence guarantee for each assignment in set constraints. Based on the mixture representation of the assignments, we further extend the analysis from fixed observations to general set constraints. The detailed contributions of this paper are: Theoretical Guarantees on General Score-Mismatched Discrete Diffusion Models : Upon characterizing the score mismatch for discrete diffusion models, we provide the first non-asymptotic convergence upper bound in KL-divergence between the target (mismatched) and the sampling distributions. Beyond the intrinsic sampling error when there is no mismatch, our theory characterizes a bias term induced by the score mismatch that arises from using the score of the training distribution to sample from a target (mismatched) distribution. Unlike the analysis in the continuous diffusion setting where the mismatch is expressed through the perturbation in the reverse Gaussian mean [ 7 ] , the mismatch for our setting perturbs the reverse rate matrix of the continuous time Markov chain (CTMC). Moreover, the Bregman divergence term associated with score entropy differs from the usual L 2 L^{2} error for the continuous setting, introducing additional complications in the analysis. Bias Characterization of Conditional SEDD: Based on the general score mismatch analysis, we further provide the first theoretical guarantees for the classical Conditional SEDD algorithm [ 9 ] under a fixed observation. By comparing the hard clamp score with the true conditional score, we reveal that the effect of hard clamping depends on the diffusion process. Under the absorbing rate, these two scores are identical on unobserved coordinates given the fixed non-MASK observation, and thus the convergence bound does not contain an additional score-mismatch bias term. Under the uniform rate, the hard clamping can introduce score mismatch over unobserved coordinates. With the assumption of condition compatibility, we bound this bias and characterize the dependence on the unobserved coordinates, vocabulary size, and compatibility parameter. Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) for Set Constraints: We propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for the set-constraint setting. In particular, we consider the setting where each constrained index in Ω ¯ \bar{\Omega} admits several candidate values from the admissible sets rather than a single fixed value. As a result, the target conditional distribution admits an exact mixture representation according to the assignments. We further show that the exact assignment distribution can be reconstructed based on the unconditional score for absorbing-rate CTMCs. As a result, the proposed RHC sampler achieves zero-shot generation with a pretrained unconditional discrete diffusion model. The numerical simulations and real-data experiments further support our theoretical results and validate the practical effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler.

sections.heading: I-B Related Works
sections.text: In this section, we focus on related works for convergence analyses and conditional generation for discrete diffusion models. Other related works on conditional continuous diffusion are provided in Appendix A . Score-matched Discrete Diffusion Model: The existing discrete diffusion analysis focuses on the score-matched setting, that is, the target distribution is consistent with the training distribution. In particular, several recent works have established non-asymptotic convergence guarantees under different noise and sampling schemes [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . However, these results cannot be directly applied when the target distribution differs from the training distribution, as in the zero-shot conditional generation. Guided Discrete Diffusion Model: Recent works have studied guidance mechanisms in discrete diffusion. [ 14 ] proposed predictor guidance and predictor-free guidance applicable to CTMC-based discrete diffusion. Their method realized the guidance through scaling the rate matrix. [ 21 ] directly derived the classifier-based and classifier-free guidance rules by reweighting the transition kernel in discrete diffusion. For conditional sampling at large, there are several strands of work. [ 22 ] proposed a discrete training-free guidance framework. [ 23 ] extended the training-free guidance to multimodal data. [ 24 ] pointed out that the bias exists in common discrete guidance methods and adopted Sequential Monte Carlo for debiasing. In addition, [ 25 ] studied reward optimization in the discrete diffusion. Similarly, [ 26 ] proposed soft value-based decoding, which introduced the soft value function to guide the model to approximate the optimal policy to implement conditional generation. These studies focus on how to incorporate conditional information into the sampling process. Our work provides a general convergence framework to explicitly quantify the additional sampling error introduced by the mismatch. Zero-Shot Discrete Diffusion Model: Zero-shot sampling has recently been explored in the discrete diffusion model. SEDD and RADD support zero-shot text infilling by fixing the prompt at each sampling step instead of retraining for the condition [ 9 , 27 ] . A discrete diffusion model based on heat bath dynamics, developed by [ 10 ] , reported good performance in zero-shot tasks, such as text and image infilling. [ 28 ] proposed a training-free method to calibrate the confidence of the sequence length to allow the adaptive length of the generated sequence. [ 29 ] proposed a plug-and-play posterior sampling method based on split Gibbs sampling. Their method introduces external conditions through the likelihood or reward guidance. Finally, note that all the works mentioned above focused mainly on algorithmic design and empirical performance, but did not characterize the theoretical performance introduced by modifications to the sampling process. Our work establishes non-asymptotic convergence guarantees to quantify how the score mismatch affects the convergence of zero-shot conditional sampling with absorbing and uniform rates. This framework further supports the analysis for set constraints. Constrained Diffusion Models: There are several studies regarding the explicit constraint for diffusion models. In continuous diffusion, [ 30 ] formulate the sampling process as an optimization problem to guide the generation result to satisfy the constraints. Using a similar idea, [ 31 ] introduced Constrained Discrete Diffusion. They incorporated differentiable projection and the augmented Lagrangian method into the sampling process so that the generated samples satisfy the conditional constraints. On the application side, [ 32 ] proposed a constrained decoding method applicable to the diffusion language model, which aims to make the generation result conform to the context-free grammar. For set constraints, our RHC uses the unconditional score to assign probabilities to feasible values. The convergence guarantee separates the assignment distribution error and the sampling error.

sections.text: In this section, we first review the basic concepts of score-matched discrete diffusion models. Then we extend it to general score-mismatched discrete diffusion models. Finally, we specialize this framework to conditional generation problems and zero-shot methods.

For this scenario, we do not aim to sample from the unconditional distribution q 0 q_{0} ; instead, our goal is to complete the unobserved parts of a sequence given the condition of observing the partial sequence. sections.text: In this section, we present the results for the convergence analysis of general score-mismatched discrete diffusion model for a general target distribution q ~ 0 \tilde{q}_{0} . sections.heading: IV-B Conditional SEDD under Fixed Observations with Uniform Rate
sections.text: In this section, we provide the convergence analysis for Conditional SEDD with the uniform rate in Theorem IV.3 . Unlike absorbing rate, uniform-rate CTMC assigns non-zero probabilities between the different clean tokens. Thus, conditioning x t Ω ¯ = y x_{t}^{\bar{\Omega}}=y at time t t does not directly imply x 0 Ω ¯ = y x_{0}^{\bar{\Omega}}=y . The hard clamp score used by Conditional SEDD will be influenced by the contributions of different clean observations. An example is provided in Appendix I to illustrate this. This distinction can introduce score mismatch to the unobserved coordinates Ω \Omega . Under the setting with the uniform rate, we first employ the following assumption to control this variation: Assumption IV.2 . For the fixed observation y ∈ [ S ] | Ω ¯ | y\in[S]^{|\bar{\Omega}|} , there exists a constant 0 < γ < 1 0<\gamma<1 such that q 0 ​ ( x 0 Ω ¯ = y | x 0 Ω ) ≥ γ , ∀ x 0 Ω ∈ supp ⁡ ( q 0 Ω ) q_{0}(x_{0}^{\bar{\Omega}}=y|x_{0}^{\Omega})\geq\gamma,\quad\forall x_{0}^{\Omega}\in\mathrm{supp}(q^{\Omega}_{0}) Assumption IV.2 requires that, given any unobserved part x 0 Ω x_{0}^{\Omega} , the likelihood of the fixed observation y y always has a positive lower bound γ \gamma . Intuitively, this assumption quantifies the compatibility between the fixed observation y y and all possible completions. Specifically, if there exists a completion x 0 Ω x_{0}^{\Omega} such that q 0 ​ ( x 0 Ω ¯ = y | x 0 Ω ) = 0 q_{0}(x_{0}^{\bar{\Omega}}=y|x_{0}^{\Omega})=0 , this completion has zero probability and is excluded from the target. In text generation tasks constrained by context, this assumption therefore allows the context to prefer some completions but requires other completions to remain possible. Such a uniform positive lower bound exists for a finite-state distribution with full support. For example, in structured text generation, y y can represent the commonly used conventional expressions such that γ \gamma is non-negligible. The second term refers to the additional bias induced by score mismatch, which reflects the cost of infilling. sections.heading: VI Experiment Results
sections.text: In this section, we provide experiment results to validate the results obtained in this paper.

sections.heading: VI-A Conditional SEDD under Fixed Observation
sections.text: In our simulation, we conduct numerical experiments on a finite data distribution q 0 q_{0} under a fixed observation x 0 Ω ¯ = y x_{0}^{\bar{\Omega}}=y . The data distribution is constructed using normalized exponential weights, resulting in a non-uniform distribution with coordinate dependencies. Upon choosing a data distribution, we estimate the corresponding KL divergence between the target distribution and the sampling distribution from the samples. More details about our settings can be found in Section J-A . To verify our theory, we first compare Conditional SEDD in [ 9 ] with the oracle sampler under absorbing and uniform rates. The oracle sampler uses the true conditional score s t | y s_{t|y} of the corresponding target distribution. Figures 1 and 2 show the comparison of the KL divergence of Conditional SEDD and the oracle sampler. Next, to further explore the effects of | Ω | |\Omega| and γ \gamma for uniform-rate Conditional SEDD, we compare the performance of Conditional SEDD with different numbers of free coordinates. The results are reported in Figure 3 . Fig. 1: Comparison of the Conditional SEDD and Oracle with fixed observation under absorbing rate in terms of the final KL divergence between the target and sampling conditional distributions. Figure 1 shows that the Conditional SEDD is closely aligned with the oracle sampler under the absorbing rate. Both errors decrease as the number of reverse time steps increases. This observation is consistent with Theorem IV.1 , where the hard-clamped score coincides with the true conditional score on Ω \Omega . Thus, Conditional SEDD introduces no additional structural score-mismatch bias for the generated results. Fig. 2: Comparison of the Conditional SEDD and Oracle with fixed observation under uniform rate in terms of the final KL divergence between the target and sampling conditional distributions. Under the uniform rate, Figure 2 shows a different phenomenon. Although the KL divergences of both samplers gradually decrease, the Conditional SEDD is stuck on an irreducible plateau for a large number of steps, and the oracle sampler achieves a smaller KL divergence. This observation is consistent with the score mismatch issue in Theorem IV.3 , where Conditional SEDD introduces an additional bias term. Thus, these results illustrate that the mismatch between Conditional SEDD and the oracle sampler will not be eliminated even with a finer time discretization. Fig. 3: Comparison of Conditional SEDD with different numbers of free coordinates under the uniform rate in terms of the final KL divergence between the target and sampling conditional distributions. The different sizes of Ω \Omega are 1 1 , 2 2 , 3 3 . Figure 3 illustrates the trends of the KL divergence of uniform-rate Conditional SEDD with different fixed observations and numbers of unobserved coordinates. For y = [ 0 ] y=[0] , [ 0 , 2 ] [0,2] , and [ 0 , 2 , 2 ] [0,2,2] , the KL divergence increases with the larger size of the unobserved set. However, with y = [ 0 , 2 , 1 ] y=[0,2,1] , the KL divergence is the worst among the four settings. The different trends across these settings do not contradict the theoretical bound in Theorem IV.3 , since the upper bound depends on both the number of free coordinates | Ω | |\Omega| and the condition compatibility parameter γ \gamma in Assumption IV.2 . As the condition changes from y = [ 0 , 2 , 2 ] y=[0,2,2] to [ 0 , 2 , 1 ] [0,2,1] , we observe a significant increase in KL divergence, which is consistent with Theorem IV.3 that a smaller γ \gamma will deteriorate the sampling error.

sections.heading: Synthetic Experiments
sections.text: For the synthetic experiments, we use the same distribution above and impose the set constraints. We compare our RHC in Algorithm 1 with the oracle sampler under absorbing-rate CTMC. The assignment probabilities w ⁡ ( a ) w(a) are computed from the exact unconditional scores. Fig. 4: Comparison of the RHC and Oracle in terms of the final KL divergence between the target and sampling conditional distributions. Figure 4 shows the comparison of the KL divergence of the oracle sampler and RHC. We evaluate the KL divergence on the generated coordinates without early stopping. In this experiment, since the assignment distribution can be calculated from the data distribution, there is no approximation error in the assignment distribution. In particular, w = v w=v and ε score path = 0 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{score}}^{\mathrm{path}}=0 . Therefore, the bound in Theorem V.3 reduces to ℰ oracle \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{oracle}} . As shown in Figure 4 , the KL divergence of both methods decreases as the number of steps increases, and RHC achieves sampling errors comparable to those of the oracle sampler. This result demonstrates the performance of RHC with the ideal constructions of the assignment distribution and the exact unconditional scores, corroborating the results in Theorem V.3 . Moreover, hard clamping in RHC introduces no score mismatch for each assignment in this experiment with the absorbing rate.

sections.heading: Text Experiments
sections.text: Beyond synthetic data, we also conduct a series of text infilling experiments with coordinatewise set constraints to validate the effectiveness of our RHC sampler. In our experiments, several positions in the sequence are selected as the constrained coordinates, where multiple candidate tokens are included (see the detailed list in Table II ). The sampler is required to select a feasible assignment for these positions in the different scenarios and generate the remaining tokens. We compare RHC with a uniform-assignment baseline. Different from RHC that selects assignments using the assignment distributions calculated from the trained unconditional scores, the baseline method samples the feasible assignments independently and uniformly. Detailed settings are shown in Section J-B . We report the generative perplexity, which is widely used to evaluate the quality of the generated text [ 9 , 21 , 27 , 34 ] , of the proposed RHC sampler and the baseline sampler in Table I . sections.heading: VII Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we have provided the convergence guarantees for the general score-mismatched discrete diffusion model. Based on the general results, we have further studied the zero-shot conditional generation. Our analysis characterizes the bias of Conditional SEDD under the fixed observations. We have shown that the hard clamp score coincides with the true conditional score under the absorbing rate case but not under the uniform rate case. We have derived an additional score-mismatched bias term in the KL upper bound under the uniform rate. To further extend conditional sampling to coordinate-wise set constraints, we have designed a novel Randomized Hard Clamping sampler with an absorbing rate. A natural direction for future work is to extend the current analysis and samplers to more general multimodal data and more complex constraint information.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Works
sections.text: Conditional Continuous Diffusion Model There exists sufficient research that focuses on the conditional generation related to the continuous diffusion model. These studies are primarily divided into two fields. One field focuses mainly on the guidance mechanism. For example, [ 35 ] proposed classifier guidance, which utilized an external classifier to modify the score function to inject conditional information into the diffusion model. [ 36 ] introduced classifier-free guidance, which combined an unconditional diffusion and a conditional diffusion to achieve conditional generation and eliminate the classifier. [ 37 ] introduced the CLIP model to measure the similarity between images and text, which can therefore be used as external guidance in diffusion models. [ 38 ] further studied the guidance mechanism in text-to-image generation and compared CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance. [ 39 ] modified the score function for the image editing area through the CLIP guidance and used the unconditional diffusion for the non-editing area. Another field is based on the unconditional diffusion without extra training. SDEdit [ 40 ] realized the image synthesis and editing by noising and denoising the user input. This method was trained on unlabeled data without retraining on the new input or tasks. RePaint [ 41 ] fixed the noised pixels to constrain the sampling process and achieve conditional generation. [ 42 ] theoretically analyzed the RePaint [ 41 ] and proposed RePaint+ to correct the bias induced by RePaint [ 41 ] . [ 43 ] proposed the ILVR method to implement image generation given reference images. This method refined the latent variables in the unconditional process to approximate the conditional process. DDRM in [ 44 ] solved the linear inverse problem by the posterior sampling based on a pretrained diffusion model, and further DPS in [ 45 ] extended the posterior sampling method to the general inverse problem. DDNM and DDNM+ [ 46 ] are also well-known zero-shot frameworks that only rely on the pretrained diffusion model. For the theoretical works, [ 7 ] provided the theoretical guarantee of the zero-shot conditional diffusion model by introducing the score mismatch concept under the continuous state cases. In addition, [ 47 , 48 , 49 ] designed the specialized conditional frameworks in the diffusion model to implement the conditional generation rather than to solely control the inference process.

Abstract Discrete diffusion models have become a powerful framework for modeling complex discrete distributions across a range of applications. While theoretical convergence guarantees depend on consistency between the target and training distributions, such a case rarely holds in practice, making score mismatch a central challenge in discrete diffusion sampling. This is particularly relevant to zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is directly reused at inference time to sample from a conditional target distribution. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis for score-mismatched discrete diffusion models and derive a general KL divergence upper bound that clearly identifies the additional bias caused by such a mismatch. Our analysis covers partial-observation constraints, including text infilling, sentence completion, and more general coordinatewise set constraints. Specifically, we analyze the classical Conditional SEDD sampler and show that it can incur a bias term that scales with the dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility. Based on this analysis, we propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints. We show that the assignment probabilities can be expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Finally, numerical and real-data experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler. Index Terms: Convergence analysis, discrete diffusion, score mismatch, set constraints, zero-shot conditional generation. I Introduction In recent years, diffusion model has become one of the core paradigms in generative modeling and has achieved impressive success in image, audio, and text generation. Compared with the classical autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion models model the complex data distribution through gradual denoising, demonstrating the notable advantages in generation quality, stability, and flexibility [ 1 , 2 ] . For discrete data such as text sequences, discrete diffusion models extend this denoising principle to the discrete case by defining the noising and denoising processes directly on the discrete state space [ 3 , 4 ] . In an idealized setting, diffusion models are trained and evaluated on the same underlying distribution. However, in practice, this assumption often fails, as discrepancies between the training and target distributions can arise due to factors such as privacy constraints, computational limitations, and mismatches between the training setup and the intended sampling task [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . A representative example is conditional generation, where part of the data is observed and the goal is to infer the unobserved part. Many tasks involving discrete data fall into this category, including sequence completion and text infilling [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Such tasks include generating the subsequent content based on the given prefix and filling the missing content while preserving the context. We refer to conditioning on fixed values as sampling “under fixed observations.” More generally, each constrained coordinate may admit several candidate values, which leads to sampling under the coordinate wise set constraints. We call a feasible combination of values an “assignment”. For example, in text rewriting and lexical simplification, each position of the word can be associated with a set of candidate replacements [ 12 , 13 ] . Fixed observations are recovered when each set contains a single value. Compared to AR models, diffusion models are more naturally suited to these tasks, as they do not rely on a fixed generation order and can flexibly handle partially observed inputs. Within conditional sampling, one solution is to train a dedicated conditional diffusion model or adapt a pretrained model for each task, such as predictor-free guidance [ 14 ] and inference-time alignment methods [ 15 ] . However, such approaches may be costly because they require additional training of a new conditional model beyond unconditional pretraining. In comparison, zero-shot conditional generation does not require such an additional conditional model, since it directly uses the given condition at inference time to build a conditional sampler [ 9 , 10 ] . The core challenge for zero-shot conditional samplers is the inherent mismatch between the pretrained unconditional model and the conditional model needed in the inference process. In diffusion sampling, this discrepancy manifests in the score function, a phenomenon known as score mismatch [ 7 ] . Among all zero-shot conditional samplers, the Conditional SEDD method [ 9 ] is particularly relevant to this paper. At each diffusion sampling step, Conditional SEDD enforces the fixed observations by setting the corresponding components of the current sample to their observed values, an operation we refer to as “hard clamping.” Although this method is straightforward to implement in practice, we will show that it is not generally equivalent to the true conditional reverse process, thereby introducing bias. Moreover, this approach still lacks any theoretical justifications. This naturally raises the first question studied in this paper: Question 1: Can we characterize the bias induced by score-mismatched discrete diffusion models? Moving from fixed observations to set constraints introduces another challenge, that is, how to allocate sampling probabilities to each feasible assignment. Once an assignment is selected, the fixed-observation sampler can be reused to generate the remaining contents. After understanding the construction of the assignment distribution, in order to make the fixed-observation sampler better aligned with the target distribution given set constraints while preserving the main advantage of the zero-shot approach, the second question arises: Question 2: Can we design a novel method that extends the fixed-observation sampler to the set constraints setting, while explicitly controlling the additional approximation error? In this paper, we answer both questions affirmatively. I-A Our Contributions Overall, our analysis focuses on how mismatched scores interfere with the reverse rate matrix, thereby introducing bias into the sampling process for both general and zero-shot conditional samplers. This analysis provides the convergence guarantee for each assignment in set constraints. Based on the mixture representation of the assignments, we further extend the analysis from fixed observations to general set constraints. The detailed contributions of this paper are: Theoretical Guarantees on General Score-Mismatched Discrete Diffusion Models : Upon characterizing the score mismatch for discrete diffusion models, we provide the first non-asymptotic convergence upper bound in KL-divergence between the target (mismatched) and the sampling distributions. Beyond the intrinsic sampling error when there is no mismatch, our theory characterizes a bias term induced by the score mismatch that arises from using the score of the training distribution to sample from a target (mismatched) distribution. Unlike the analysis in the continuous diffusion setting where the mismatch is expressed through the perturbation in the reverse Gaussian mean [ 7 ] , the mismatch for our setting perturbs the reverse rate matrix of the continuous time Markov chain (CTMC). Moreover, the Bregman divergence term associated with score entropy differs from the usual L 2 L^{2} error for the continuous setting, introducing additional complications in the analysis. Bias Characterization of Conditional SEDD: Based on the general score mismatch analysis, we further provide the first theoretical guarantees for the classical Conditional SEDD algorithm [ 9 ] under a fixed observation. By comparing the hard clamp score with the true conditional score, we reveal that the effect of hard clamping depends on the diffusion process. Under the absorbing rate, these two scores are identical on unobserved coordinates given the fixed non-MASK observation, and thus the convergence bound does not contain an additional score-mismatch bias term. Under the uniform rate, the hard clamping can introduce score mismatch over unobserved coordinates. With the assumption of condition compatibility, we bound this bias and characterize the dependence on the unobserved coordinates, vocabulary size, and compatibility parameter. Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) for Set Constraints: We propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for the set-constraint setting. In particular, we consider the setting where each constrained index in Ω ¯  ar{\Omega} admits several candidate values from the admissible sets rather than a single fixed value. As a result, the target conditional distribution admits an exact mixture representation according to the assignments. We further show that the exact assignment distribution can be reconstructed based on the unconditional score for absorbing-rate CTMCs. As a result, the proposed RHC sampler achieves zero-shot generation with a pretrained unconditional discrete diffusion model. The numerical simulations and real-data experiments further support our theoretical results and validate the practical effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler. I-B Related Works In this section, we focus on related works for convergence analyses and conditional generation for discrete diffusion models. Other related works on conditional continuous diffusion are provided in Appendix A . Score-matched Discrete Diffusion Model: The existing discrete diffusion analysis focuses on the score-matched setting, that is, the target distribution is consistent with the training distribution. In particular, several recent works have established non-asymptotic convergence guarantees under different noise and sampling schemes [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . However, these results cannot be directly applied when the target distribution differs from the training distribution, as in the zero-shot conditional generation. Guided Discrete Diffusion Model: Recent works have studied guidance mechanisms in discrete diffusion. [ 14 ] proposed predictor guidance and predictor-free guidance applicable to CTMC-based discrete diffusion. Their method realized the guidance through scaling the rate matrix. [ 21 ] directly derived the classifier-based and classifier-free guidance rules by reweighting the transition kernel in discrete diffusion. For conditional sampling at large, there are several strands of work. [ 22 ] proposed a discrete training-free guidance framework. [ 23 ] extended the training-free guidance to multimodal data. [ 24 ] pointed out that the bias exists in common discrete guidance methods and adopted Sequential Monte Carlo for debiasing. In addition, [ 25 ] studied reward optimization in the discrete diffusion. Similarly, [ 26 ] proposed soft value-based decoding, which introduced the soft value function to guide the model to approximate the optimal policy to implement conditional generation. These studies focus on how to incorporate conditional information into the sampling process. Our work provides a general convergence framework to explicitly quantify the additional sampling error introduced by the mismatch. Zero-Shot Discrete Diffusion Model: Zero-shot sampling has recently been explored in the discrete diffusion model. SEDD and RADD support zero-shot text infilling by fixing the prompt at each sampling step instead of retraining for the condition [ 9 , 27 ] . A discrete diffusion model based on heat bath dynamics, developed by [ 10 ] , reported good performance in zero-shot tasks, such as text and image infilling. [ 28 ] proposed a training-free method to calibrate the confidence of the sequence length to allow the adaptive length of the generated sequence. [ 29 ] proposed a plug-and-play posterior sampling method based on split Gibbs sampling. Their method introduces external conditions through the likelihood or reward guidance. Finally, note that all the works mentioned above focused mainly on algorithmic design and empirical performance, but did not characterize the theoretical performance introduced by modifications to the sampling process. Our work establishes non-asymptotic convergence guarantees to quantify how the score mismatch affects the convergence of zero-shot conditional sampling with absorbing and uniform rates. This framework further supports the analysis for set constraints. Constrained Diffusion Models: There are several studies regarding the explicit constraint for diffusion models. In continuous diffusion, [ 30 ] formulate the sampling process as an optimization problem to guide the generation result to satisfy the constraints. Using a similar idea, [ 31 ] introduced Constrained Discrete Diffusion. They incorporated differentiable projection and the augmented Lagrangian method into the sampling process so that the generated samples satisfy the conditional constraints. On the application side, [ 32 ] proposed a constrained decoding method applicable to the diffusion language model, which aims to make the generation result conform to the context-free grammar. For set constraints, our RHC uses the unconditional score to assign probabilities to feasible values. The convergence guarantee separates the assignment distribution error and the sampling error.
